content: Kidney stones are a common condition globally and have a high likelihood of recurring, even after treatment. Recurrence is particularly frequent in individuals with low levels of urinary citrate. These individuals are more prone to developing calcium phosphate and calcium oxalate stones. Oral citrate therapy works by increasing urinary citrate levels, which then bind to calcium, inhibiting crystal formation and reducing the likelihood of stone development. Despite its widespread use for preventing and treating calcium oxalate stones, the clinical efficacy of oral citrate therapy remains uncertain. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and potential adverse effects of citrate salts in the treatment and prevention of calcium-containing kidney stones. To achieve this, a systematic search was conducted in the Cochrane Kidney and Transplant Specialized Register up to July 29, 2015, using relevant search terms. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that assessed the efficacy and adverse events of citrate salts in adults treated for at least six months. Seven studies involving a total of 477 participants were included in the review. Most participants had calcium oxalate stones. Among these studies, three (247 participants) compared potassium citrate with placebo or no intervention, three (166 participants) compared potassium-sodium citrate with no intervention, and one (64 participants) compared potassium-magnesium citrate with placebo. The overall quality of the included studies was rated as moderate to poor, with a high risk of attrition bias in two studies. Citrate therapy was found to significantly reduce stone size compared to placebo or no intervention (4 studies, 160 participants: risk ratio [RR] 2.35, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.36 to 4.05). Additionally, the formation of new stones was significantly lower in the citrate therapy group compared to the control group (7 studies, 324 participants: RR 0.26, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.68). Citrate therapy also demonstrated a beneficial effect on stabilizing stone size (4 studies, 160 participants: RR 1.97, 95% CI 1.19 to 3.26). Adverse events were reported in four studies, with the most common side effects being upper gastrointestinal disturbances. One patient reported a rash. Although gastrointestinal side effects were more frequent in the citrate group, this difference was not statistically significant (4 studies, 271 participants: RR 2.55, 95% CI 0.71 to 9.16). However, significantly more participants in the citrate group discontinued treatment due to adverse events compared to the control group (4 studies, 271 participants: RR 4.45, 95% CI 1.28 to 15.50). The need for retreatment was significantly lower in the citrate therapy group compared to the control group (2 studies, 157 participants: RR 0.22, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.89). In conclusion, citrate salts are effective in preventing the formation of new stones and reducing the growth of residual stones, particularly those containing calcium oxalate. However, the quality of the available evidence is moderate to poor. Therefore, a well-designed, adequately powered, multi-center randomized controlled trial is necessary to address key questions regarding the efficacy of citrate salts.
